findings.paper_title: Short to Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027-29
findings.headline: Balanced 2026/27 budget approved in February required £0.7m adjustment within 7 months due to emerging pay re-grading cost of £621k (recurring)
findings.detail: Council approved a balanced budget for 2026/27 on 25 February 2026. By September 2026, emerging pressures totalling £851k forced adjustment, particularly a pay re-grading creating £621k recurring cost. Partially offset by insurance savings (£342k) and loans savings (£250k), but net result is £726k additional 2026/27 savings target. The recurring nature means this flows forward into 2027/28.
findings.matters: A 'balanced' budget that required material adjustment within 7 months shows underlying budget discipline challenges. The recurring pay cost is a structural increase that will complicate future budget balancing. Lenders need confidence in budget forecasting accuracy.
findings.figures: Emerging pressures £851k; pay re-grading £621k (recurring); insurance saving £342k; loans saving £250k; additional savings target £726k
findings.quote: Pay pressures as the result of a role re-grading as reported in Q4 2025/26 have resulted in a recurring budget pressure of £621,000.

findings.paper_title: Short to Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027-29
findings.headline: No Scottish Government pay policy published beyond 2025/28 framework; budget assumes 3% pay growth but outcome uncertain and pay is budget's most sensitive variable (1% variance = £1.3m impact)
findings.detail: The Council assumes 3% pay awards for planning but 'no Scottish Government pay policy has been published beyond the current 2025/26 to 2027/28 framework.' A recent pay re-grading has already created £621k of recurring cost. Pay represents the largest controllable cost item. Budget sensitivity analysis shows 1% variance in pay costs = £1.3m impact, making this a material risk.
findings.matters: Pay is approximately 60% of council spending. Uncertainty over future pay policy makes forecasting difficult, and awards higher than assumed would rapidly exhaust financial flexibility and increase budget gaps.
findings.figures: 3% pay award assumption; pay re-grading created £621k recurring cost; budget sensitivity to 1% pay variance = £1.3m impact
findings.quote: At the time of preparing this Strategy, no Scottish Government pay policy has been published beyond the current 2025/26 to 2027/28 framework. Whilst Scottish Government has indicated that a review of public sector pay policy will form part of the 2027/28 Budget process, the outcome remains uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Short to Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027-29
findings.headline: Council Tax policy beyond 2026/27 not confirmed by Scottish Government; budget assumes 6% increase generating £3.8m, but freeze or cap would worsen gap significantly
findings.detail: The 2027/28 budget assumes Council Tax will increase by 6%, providing £3.8m of additional income. However, the Scottish Government has not confirmed policy beyond 2026/27. The document explicitly warns that any freeze or cap without full compensation 'would increase the budget gap and require additional savings, income generation or use of reserves.' Given recent history of Council Tax freezes, this is a material risk entirely outside the council's control.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the council's second-largest funding source. Any reduction without compensation would directly increase the budget gap by millions and force rapid service decisions. Policy risk over a major income stream is a material lender concern.
findings.figures: Council Tax 2026/27 £63.6m; 2027/28 £67.8m (assuming 6% increase); 6% increase generates £3.8m additional income
findings.quote: The Scottish Government has not yet provided certainty regarding Council Tax policy beyond 2026/27. Whilst there has been no formal announcement of a freeze or cap on future Council Tax increases, the possibility of further national intervention cannot be discounted.

findings.paper_title: Short to Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027-29
findings.headline: Transformation programme savings are front-loaded and limited: £447k (2026/27) dropping to £149k (2027/28) and £0 (2028/29), leaving £726k still to identify in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Council's strategy relies on transformation as the preferred lever, but actual savings delivery is concentrated in 2026/27 with minimal ongoing benefit. Many proposed savings remain aspirational or unquantified (workforce review, demand-led reductions, best value analysis, partnership contributions). If projects don't deliver or savings proposals can't be implemented, gaps will widen and force harder service reduction choices.
findings.matters: Delivery risk on savings plans directly impacts whether the council can close its budget gaps. If transformation projects plateau or fail, the council faces either larger unmanaged deficits or more severe service cuts. Lenders need to see credible, quantified delivery mechanisms.
findings.figures: Transformation savings: 2026/27 £447k; 2027/28 £149k; 2028/29 £0k. Savings still to be identified 2026/27: £726k. Total 2026/27 savings required: £5,357k.
findings.quote: Where expenditure is potentially recurring, budget managers will be asked to develop plans for service reduction to bring expenditure into line with budget. This could be from reduction in services standards, reduction in volume of service or from alternative methods of service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Short to Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027-29
findings.headline: MIJB health and social care partnership faces cost pressures but budget assumes no increase in Council's £4.2m annual subsidy
findings.detail: The Council subsidises the Moray Integration Joint Board (health and social care) to the tune of £4.2m annually, and the budget assumes this remains flat. However, the document explicitly notes that increased pay awards, general inflation, and increased demand (particularly for out-of-area children's placements) are forecast, and 'There is the risk that expenditure may not be contained.' Any increase in MIJB costs would flow directly to the council's budget gap.
findings.matters: MIJB is a major cost (£4.2m shortfall funding alone) that the Council cannot fully control. Cost overruns by a partnership body would directly worsen the council's budget position and reduce financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £4,200,000 MIJB shortfall funding assumed flat; no increase provided for despite identified pressures
findings.quote: The indicative budget assumes no increase in the shortfall funding for MIJB which currently stands at £4,200,000. The MIJB plans for containing costs may not be deliverable within the required timescales.

findings.paper_title: Short to Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027-29
findings.headline: Budget gaps have deteriorated since February: 2027/28 now £3.1m (was £2.9m), 2028/29 now £8.5m (was £7.4m)
findings.detail: Forecasts of budget shortfalls have worsened in all years. The 2027/28 gap has increased by £0.2m and 2028/29 by £1.1m since budgets were set in February. To manage this risk, the Council has set a £2.5m savings target for 2027/28 — well above the indicative gap — to create a buffer against further adverse variances in key assumptions.
findings.matters: Growing budget gaps indicate the council's financial position is deteriorating faster than forecast, directly affecting its ability to balance the budget or maintain service levels. Lenders need confidence in credible closure plans.
findings.quote: The Strategy notes the potential significant impact of variances from budget assumptions and sets a tolerance level to increase the projected savings to be identified to allow for the impact of a moderate variance from base assumptions and on that basis sets a savings target for 2027/28 of £2.5m.

findings.paper_title: Short to Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027-29
findings.headline: Loan charges forecast to rise to £2.4m (2027/28) and £5.0m (2028/29), up from £0.3m in 2026/27, creating a major structural revenue pressure
findings.detail: The Council's capital spending is creating rising annual debt service costs. After a small 2026/27 saving from capital underspend, loan charges increase sharply to £2.4m in 2027/28 and £5.0m in 2028/29. This is a structural cost that cannot be avoided without reducing capital programmes, and will make future budget gaps much harder to close.
findings.matters: Debt service is an unavoidable cost that must be met from revenue. Rising loan charges constrain financial flexibility and reduce the council's ability to invest or absorb other pressures. A lender would track whether these costs can be serviced sustainably.
findings.quote: An underspend in the Capital Plan from 2025/26 creates a reduction in expected loans recharges for 2026/27. Accounting for the underspend, offset by potential interest rate risk, a reduction in loans charges of £250,000 is recommended to be reflected in the budget figure.

findings.paper_title: Regeneration Capital Grant Fund 2027-28 Additional Applications
findings.headline: The £38m St Giles Shopping Centre project involves a Council-owned asset with financial and operational implications yet to be assessed.
findings.detail: The St Giles project is a £38.3m programme involving Council property. The Council defers assessment of "property, operational, financial and legal implications" until Stage 2. Full project details are in a confidential report.
findings.matters: A large capital project requires committed match funding (£3.96m) and Council involvement with property implications, yet full implications remain unassessed despite lead applicant status.
findings.figures: Total project cost £38,274,010; RCGF request £1,000,000; match funding needed £3,960,000
findings.quote: Should the project progress beyond Stage 1, any property, operational, financial and legal implications associated with the Council-owned asset would be subject to further consideration and approval through the appropriate Council governance process.

findings.paper_title: Regeneration Capital Grant Fund 2027-28 Additional Applications
findings.headline: The four projects require £10.3m in match funding that is not secured and does not represent a Council commitment.
findings.detail: Match funding totalling £10.3m is required across the four projects, ranging from £272k to £3.96m per project. The paper explicitly states these amounts "do not represent a commitment by Moray Council to provide the funding." Sources are not identified.
findings.matters: If projects progress to Stage 2, the Council faces pressure to identify and commit substantial match funding for capital projects; this creates future uncertain financial exposure.
findings.figures: Total match funding requirement £10,320,669; largest requirement St Giles £3,960,000
findings.quote: Match funding figures represent the balance of anticipated project costs and do not represent a commitment by Moray Council to provide the funding.

findings.paper_title: Regeneration Capital Grant Fund 2027-28 Additional Applications
findings.headline: As lead applicant for four capital grant proposals, the Council faces financial and compliance liability if grant conditions are not met or project promoters cannot deliver.
findings.detail: The Council explicitly acknowledges exposure to financial risk across the four projects if grant conditions are breached or project partners fail to perform. This creates contingent liability on the Council's financial position.
findings.matters: Lead applicant status creates potential contractual obligations that the Council must manage; this is material contingent liability affecting financial risk.
findings.figures: Total project costs £48,741,239; total RCGF request £4,746,560 across four proposals
findings.quote: However, as lead applicant, the Council may be exposed to financial risk should an application ultimately be successful and grant conditions not be met, or where project promoters are unable to fulfil their obligations.

findings.paper_title: Regeneration Capital Grant Fund 2027-28 Additional Applications
findings.headline: The St Giles Shopping Centre works lost their planned funding source and now depend on the RCGF application.
findings.detail: This project was expected to be funded through an alternative funding stream but that bid was unsuccessful. The notification came after the earlier committee report, prompting inclusion in the RCGF submission instead.
findings.matters: The Council has pivoted a planned project to grant-dependent funding, creating reliance on discretionary funding rather than a secured source.
findings.figures: St Giles RCGF request £1,000,000 from total project cost £38,274,010
findings.quote: The St Giles Shopping Centre area works were anticipated to receive support through an alternative funding stream. However, notification that the bid had been unsuccessful was received after the earlier committee report had been prepared.

findings.paper_title: Regeneration Capital Grant Fund 2027-28 Additional Applications
findings.headline: The Council submitted two additional RCGF applications without prior committee approval, requiring retrospective homologation.
findings.detail: The Council's committee schedule made it impossible to seek approval before the 14 August 2026 deadline. The Corporate Leadership Team approved submission on 6 August 2026, with commitment to seek Council homologation later. This paper seeks that homologation.
findings.matters: Councils operate under strict governance frameworks; circumventing normal approval processes—even with retrospective consent—signals governance pressure and timeline constraints that could affect decision-making.
findings.figures: Deadline 14 August 2026; CLT decision 6 August 2026
findings.quote: Due to the Stage 1 submission deadline of 14 August 2026 and the timing of the Council's committee cycle, there was insufficient opportunity to seek approval for the two additional applications through the normal committee process.

findings.paper_title: Options for Additional Council Tax Charge and Second Home Premium
findings.headline: High collection rates support confidence that additional revenue projections would be achievable
findings.detail: In-year collection rates for 2025/26 were 85.2% for the Additional Council Tax Charge and 97.7% for the Second Home Premium. These rates are materially higher than typical council tax collection, suggesting that revenue modeling is based on reliable collection experience and that increased charges would be collected effectively.
findings.matters: Strong collection provides confidence that projected revenue will materialize if charges are implemented.
findings.figures: 2025/26 in-year collection rates: 85.2% (Additional Council Tax Charge), 97.7% (Second Home Premium).
findings.quote: Collection Rates for the Additional Council Tax Charge and Second Home Premium are high.  At 31 March 2026 the 2025/26 in-year collection percentages were 85.2% and 97.7% respectively.

findings.paper_title: Options for Additional Council Tax Charge and Second Home Premium
findings.headline: Historical data shows limited behavioral response to existing charges, creating uncertainty over actual revenue gains
findings.detail: Since introducing the Additional Council Tax Charge in 2014, Moray's long-term empty properties have decreased only 7.4% (from 662 to 613). Since introducing the Second Home Premium in 2024, second homes have decreased 12.3% (from 721 to 632). The paper models potential scenarios with behavioral change but provides no evidence that higher charges will produce materially different results.
findings.matters: If behavioral response mirrors historical patterns, actual revenue could be substantially lower than projected, creating risk of overestimating income.
findings.figures: Long-term empty properties 2014-2026: 662 to 613 (7.4% decrease). Second homes 2024-2026: 721 to 632 (12.3% decrease).
findings.quote: The imposition of the Additional Council Tax Charge and the Second Home Premium as a negative 'incentive' to bring unoccupied properties back into use a main residence has only delivered minimal results.

findings.paper_title: Options for Additional Council Tax Charge and Second Home Premium
findings.headline: Council explores potential to raise £2-4M additional annual revenue from increasing discretionary council tax charges
findings.detail: Moray currently raises £0.944M from a 100% Additional Council Tax Charge on long-term empty properties and £1.033M from a 100% Second Home Premium. Modeling shows potential incremental revenue of £1.8-2.1M from the Additional Charge and £1.0-2.1M from the Second Home Premium if charges are increased to 200-300% with no behavioral change. Other Scottish councils have already implemented 200-300% levels.
findings.matters: This represents material discretionary revenue available to strengthen the council's financial position if implemented.
findings.figures: Current revenue: £0.944M (Additional Charge), £1.033M (Second Home Premium). Modeled incremental revenue at 200%: £0.944M and £1.033M respectively. Modeled incremental revenue at 300%: £1.888M and £2.066M respectively.
findings.quote: At 1 April 2026, 613 properties in Moray were subject to the levy of this charge, raising gross Council Tax revenues of £0.944M in 2026/27... At 1 April 2026, 632 properties in Moray were subject to the levy of this charge, raising gross Council Tax revenues of £1.033M in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Bus Revolution Strategic Approach and Revenue Budget Phase 3
findings.headline: The Phase 3 budget is grounded in actual FY2025/26 and FY2026/27 performance data rather than original project assumptions.
findings.detail: Rather than relying on the assumptions in the original Full Business Case, the revised Phase 3 financial model uses actual operating costs, observed passenger demand and evidenced income performance achieved through Phases 1 and 2. This reflects current operating conditions and demonstrated performance, making the budget more credible than assumption-based forecasting.
findings.matters: Evidence-based budgeting grounded in actual performance is more reliable for forecasting than assumption-driven models, reducing the risk that revenue or cost forecasts will prove incorrect.
findings.figures: Budget based on actual FY2025/26 and FY2026/27 data; forecast operating expenditure £1.160m; forecast income £473,248
findings.quote: The proposed budget has been developed using actual operating costs, observed passenger demand and evidenced income performance achieved through delivery of the m.connect network.

findings.paper_title: Bus Revolution Strategic Approach and Revenue Budget Phase 3
findings.headline: FY2025/26 subsidy variances were absorbed through underspends in other public transport budgets without requiring additional council funding.
findings.detail: While the net subsidy requirement fluctuated during FY2025/26 due to fuel market pressures, increased staffing costs and slower income maturation than forecast, the variance was managed through underspends elsewhere within the Public Transport budget and did not require any additional council funding beyond the planned £686,435.
findings.matters: Shows the council has budget flexibility to absorb operational variances in public transport without requiring emergency funding, reducing risk to the council's overall finances.
findings.figures: Subsidy fluctuated in FY2025/26 but no additional funding required; annual subsidy £686,435
findings.quote: Whilst the net subsidy fluctuated during FY2025/26, it was managed through underspends elsewhere within the Public Transport budget and did not require any additional Council funding.

findings.paper_title: Bus Revolution Strategic Approach and Revenue Budget Phase 3
findings.headline: The Scottish Government £2 fare cap, introduced March 2026, is contributing to revenue growth but its withdrawal could reduce income.
findings.detail: The £2 fare cap scheme introduced in March 2026 has contributed positively to passenger growth and farebox income performance by improving affordability whilst maintaining operator income through reimbursement. The paper identifies withdrawal or amendment of the scheme as a key external risk that could reduce passenger demand and adversely affect Phase 3 income growth assumptions.
findings.matters: The revenue model is dependent on a Scottish Government policy that could change, creating a material risk to the council's forecast income and potentially increasing subsidy requirements.
findings.figures: Fare cap introduced March 2026; Phase 3 income forecast £473,248; scheme withdrawal flagged as key external risk
findings.quote: Withdrawal or significant amendment of the scheme could reduce passenger demand and adversely affect income growth assumptions contained within the Phase 3 budget.

findings.paper_title: Bus Revolution Strategic Approach and Revenue Budget Phase 3
findings.headline: The council is maintaining its £686,435 annual subsidy despite pivoting Phase 3 from network expansion to analytical development.
findings.detail: Despite changing Phase 3 strategy from service expansion to development of data tools, performance monitoring and service optimization, the revised revenue budget maintains the existing annual subsidy commitment of £686,435. No additional council funding is required to deliver the revised Phase 3 programme.
findings.matters: Demonstrates financial discipline and evidence-based planning by the council, prioritizing analytical capability before further expansion rather than committing additional resources.
findings.figures: £686,435 annual subsidy maintained; forecast operating expenditure £1.160m; income forecast £473,248
findings.quote: The revised profile maintains the existing annual Council subsidy contribution of £686,435 whilst aligning expenditure and income assumptions with a phase focused on analysis, evaluation, optimisation and future business case development rather than network expansion.

findings.paper_title: Bus Revolution Strategic Approach and Revenue Budget Phase 3
findings.headline: Passenger journeys have grown 86% since project start and farebox income is growing at 22.6% annually.
findings.detail: Passenger journeys increased from 45,881 in 2022/23 to 85,309 in 2025/26. In the first four months of FY2026/27, passenger journeys increased 17% year-on-year whilst farebox income increased 22.6%. Revenue performance is tracking at approximately 98% of original model assumptions and is forecast to exceed £360,000 per annum.
findings.matters: Growing revenue from the service suggests it is becoming increasingly financially sustainable and reduces the council's future subsidy dependency.
findings.figures: 86% passenger growth since project start; 22.6% farebox income growth FY2026/27 YTD; forecast annual revenue exceeds £360,000
findings.quote: farebox income increased by 22.6%

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Section Update Report
findings.headline: Complex and Challenging Needs Service has control weaknesses in expense claims, procurement and financial management
findings.detail: Beyond staffing, the service has multiple control issues. These include undated travel and expense claims (approximately one-third of claims submitted without dates), non-compliance with procurement guidelines on a £25,000 bicycle shed purchase, inadequate management of personal resident cash holdings, and support plans not reviewed for over a year. The service received 'Substantial' audit assurance rather than Full. Multiple medium and low-priority recommendations remain unresolved, with some pushed to 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Multiple control weaknesses in a £7.7m service indicate governance and compliance issues that may increase financial and reputational risk
findings.figures: 1 high-priority recommendation; 8 medium-priority and 5 low-priority recommendations; 2 recommendations still outstanding/part-implemented as of August 2026
findings.quote: However, an example was noted where Guidelines had not been followed in the procurement for the purchase and installation of a bicycle shed to the value of £25,000.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Section Update Report
findings.headline: Complex and Challenging Needs Service (£7.7m budget) facing unresolved staffing crisis with high overtime costs
findings.detail: The social care service supporting individuals in two facilities has significant staffing vacancies and high overtime costs. The original audit (November 2025) and follow-up (August 2026) found that £750,000 was paid in overtime in 2024/25, with some support workers regularly exceeding 60 hours per week. The audit identified this working pattern as unsustainable. The high-priority staffing recommendation remains only 'part implemented' as of the follow-up review, with completion pushed to 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: A significant service budget with disclosed operational stress and unresolved recommendations; high overtime costs suggest service delivery risk if staffing vacancies are not resolved
findings.figures: £7.7m annual budget (2024/25); £750,000 paid in overtime (2024/25); some support workers regularly working over 60 hours per week
findings.quote: Approximately £750,000 was paid in overtime during 2024/25. Audit testing of individual overtime claims, undertaken to verify accuracy and compliance with Financial Regulations, revealed that some Support Workers are regularly working in excess of 60 hours per week.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Section Update Report
findings.headline: Levelling Up Fund (£18.29m capital program) receiving full audit assurance with appropriate governance in place
findings.detail: Moray Council was awarded £18.29m in November 2023 for town centre regeneration, transport and cultural projects. The council acts as accountable body to government. By September 2025, £8.1m had been received with £1.7m expended on project management, design and enabling works. The August 2026 follow-up audit provided full assurance on governance, financial control, risk management and administrative arrangements. All audit recommendations have been implemented.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council has secured and is appropriately managing a major government capital program with proper oversight of a significant external funding commitment
findings.figures: £18.29m awarded November 2023; £8.1m received; £1.7m expended (as of September 2025)
findings.quote: Moray Council was awarded £18.29 million in November 2023 to support town centre regeneration, transport improvements and cultural projects, with the Council acting as the accountable body responsible for financial compliance, procurement and reporting to the UK Government.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance and Treasury and Capital Investment Prudential Indicators for 2025-26
findings.headline: General Services financing costs improved in 2025/26 but forecast to worsen in 2026/27 as capital expenditure increases significantly
findings.detail: General Services financing costs improved to 8.62% in 2025/26 from 10.63%, providing headroom below the 10% affordability limit. However, the improvement was driven partly by capital programme underspend. The 2026/27 forecast shows the ratio rising to 9.27% as capital expenditure is expected to increase to £77.294m from £32.855m in 2025/26.
findings.matters: The 2025/26 improvement masks structural tightening: the council's underlying affordability position is being squeezed by rising capital needs. As the capital programme accelerates (catching up from slippage), financing costs will rise closer to the affordability ceiling.
findings.quote: For General Services, the indicator reduced from 10.63% in 2024/25 to 8.62% in 2025/26 and remained below the Council's affordability threshold of 10%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance and Treasury and Capital Investment Prudential Indicators for 2025-26
findings.headline: Total council debt increased £27.6m to £323.4m, with shift towards short-term borrowing concentrating refinancing risk
findings.detail: Total borrowing increased from £295.854m to £323.418m. Within this, temporary (short-term inter-authority) borrowing increased from £99m to £118m while long-term PWLB borrowing increased from £196.854m to £205.418m. The average life of debt shortened from 13.5 years to 11.8 years. This shift concentrates refinancing risk: when short-term loans mature, the council must refinance them, potentially at higher rates.
findings.matters: Growing debt and shortening maturity profile increase refinancing risk. If short-term rates rise or the inter-authority market becomes less available, the council could face significantly higher borrowing costs. This strategy is cost-effective only if favorable short-term rate conditions persist.
findings.figures: Total debt £295.854m to £323.418m; temporary borrowing £99m to £118m; average life 13.5 to 11.8 years
findings.quote: The availability of preferential rates within the inter-authority market resulted in an increase in the proportion of short-term borrowing during the year when compared to long-term borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance and Treasury and Capital Investment Prudential Indicators for 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs at 33.78% forecast for 2026/27, within 1.22% of the 35% approved affordability limit
findings.detail: HRA financing costs are forecast at 33.78% of revenue stream for 2026/27, up sharply from 29.06% in 2025/26. With an approved limit of 35%, the council has minimal headroom: a 1.22 percentage point increase in financing costs would reach the affordability ceiling. This could force the council to raise rents or cut housing services.
findings.matters: A local authority approaching its affordability ceiling faces constrained options if costs rise further. For a housing function already showing delivery challenges, limited affordability headroom signals vulnerability to interest rate rises or cost overruns.
findings.figures: 33.78% (2026/27 forecast) vs 35% approved limit; up from 29.06% (2025/26 actual)
findings.quote: remains within the Council's affordability threshold of 35%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance and Treasury and Capital Investment Prudential Indicators for 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing capital programme delivered at 78%, with contractor availability and resource constraints restricting delivery
findings.detail: HRA capital expenditure was £31.655m against a revised plan of £40.639m. The council explicitly attributes underspend to contractor availability, internal resource constraints, and tenant permission issues affecting housing maintenance and new-build programmes.
findings.matters: Housing investment slippage suggests operational delivery constraints and may indicate the council cannot execute its housing strategy as planned. This affects housing delivery and complicates forecasting of capital financing needs.
findings.figures: £31.655m delivered of £40.639m plan (78% delivery rate)
findings.quote: Ongoing challenges around contractor availability, internal resources and tenant permissions also affected delivery of elements of the programme.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance and Treasury and Capital Investment Prudential Indicators for 2025-26
findings.headline: General Services capital programme delivered at only 65%, with Learning Estate and Moray Growth Deal among projects being reprofiled
findings.detail: General Services capital expenditure was £32.855m against a revised capital plan of £50.564m. Major capital projects including the Learning Estate and Moray Growth Deal have been reprofiled into future years, indicating significant slippage in the council's investment plan.
findings.matters: Slippage in major capital programmes indicates either project management challenges or changes in investment priorities. This affects the council's ability to deliver infrastructure and raises questions about capacity to execute its capital plan.
findings.figures: £32.855m delivered of £50.564m plan (65% delivery rate)
findings.quote: The shortfall was largely due to the reprofiling of expenditure across a number of major capital projects, including the Learning Estate, Moray Growth Deal and other property and infrastructure projects, resulting in expenditure being carried forward into future financial years.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance and Treasury and Capital Investment Prudential Indicators for 2025-26
findings.headline: Council breached its approved prudential indicator limit for borrowing maturing within 12 months, reaching 42.74% against 37% limit
findings.detail: The council deliberately exceeded its prudential indicator for short-term borrowing maturity. £139.444m of the council's £326.256m total borrowing (42.74%) matures within 12 months, exceeding the approved upper limit of 37%. The council chose lower-cost short-term inter-authority borrowing over longer-term PWLB loans.
findings.matters: Breaching an approved prudential indicator signals the council prioritized cost savings over staying within its approved risk framework. A lender needs to understand whether such breaches will become routine and whether the council's actual risk tolerance differs from its stated limits.
findings.figures: 42.74% actual vs 37% upper limit; £139.444m of £326.256m total borrowing maturing <12 months
findings.quote: The upper limit for borrowing maturing within 12 months was exceeded during 2025/26 due to the Council's continued use of short-term inter-authority borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Commercial Harbours
findings.headline: Rental income from council-owned commercial units at harbours has not been optimized, with lease agreements not subject to rent reviews for several years despite lease conditions permitting annual review.
findings.detail: Audit review of commercial units at Buckie and Burghead Harbours found rental income accurately charged and recorded, but leases had not undergone rent review for several years despite lease conditions allowing annual review. Management explained this resulted from prioritizing review of higher-value leases. Management intends to conduct reviews across all value categories using additional temporary resources.
findings.matters: Councils are expected to optimize income from assets. Failure to conduct lease reviews represents foregone revenue, indicating incomplete financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Commercial units with leases below £1,000 per annum excluded from review process; management response target 31/12/27
findings.quote: A review of a sample of lease agreements found that these commercial units had not been subject to a rent review for several years. Lease agreement conditions allow for an annual review of rental charges.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Commercial Harbours
findings.headline: Harbour operations require ongoing overtime payments to maintain 24/7 service delivery, with management acknowledging this arrangement is not sustainable and seeking a contractual solution.
findings.detail: Audit testing identified overtime payments as ongoing. Management explained that maritime operational timescales (24/7 operations) do not align with standard council employee terms and conditions, making overtime necessary. The audit notes overtime should only be used exceptionally and temporarily, not routinely. Senior management acknowledged the issue and are pursuing a sustainable solution to contractual arrangements.
findings.matters: Routine overtime represents persistent cost pressure in service operations. If the service requires ongoing staffing overspend to operate at stated levels, this affects claimed financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Service staffed 24/7; overtime driven by operational requirements not aligned with standard employment terms
findings.quote: However, it is considered that overtime should only be used on an exceptional and temporary basis, rather than as a routine arrangement. Senior management are aware of this issue and are seeking an appropriate solution to address the current contractual arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Commercial Harbours
findings.headline: Commercial harbour operations generate approximately £1 million in income against £940,000 in operating costs, making the service roughly self-sustaining without requiring council subsidy.
findings.detail: The audit reviewed financial performance of Buckie and Burghead Harbours in 2025/26. Income streams include fishing-related activities, cargo handling, and increasingly offshore renewable energy operations. Operating costs—primarily staffing and infrastructure maintenance—are covered by user fees and grants. The service does not require council subsidy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council is subsidizing loss-making services. This operation is financially self-supporting.
findings.figures: Operating costs approximately £940,000; income approximately £1 million (2025/26 and 2026/27)
findings.quote: In 2025/26, operating costs for Buckie and Burghead Harbours were approximately £940,000, with staffing costs and infrastructure maintenance comprising the majority of expenditure. Income generated from service users, rents and grant funding totalled approximately £1 million.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Social Care (Short Breaks)
findings.headline: CareFirst (the primary financial system for social care) contains inaccurate recording of Short Breaks including missing end dates and incorrect categorisation.
findings.detail: The audit identified inaccuracies in CareFirst, the council's primary system for managing social care packages and validating payments. These included end dates not being updated when stays were extended, end dates not being entered at all, and services miscategorised. While the council is replacing CareFirst with Mosaic (implementation planned March 2027), accurate data input remains critical. Management has accepted recommendations for staff retraining, due 31 January 2027.
findings.matters: CareFirst is the primary system for validating social care payments; data quality issues undermine the reliability of financial information and the council's ability to identify errors in spending.
findings.figures: No figures provided
findings.quote: Inaccuracies included end dates not being updated to reflect approved extensions or differences between planned and actual end dates, end dates not being entered, and services not being correctly categorised as Short Breaks.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Social Care (Short Breaks)
findings.headline: Extended stays of up to 16 months are misclassified as Short Breaks, distorting budget accuracy and service planning.
findings.detail: Audit testing found spending classified as Short Break provision related to stays of 5-16 months in residential care. These extended placements were approved as interim measures pending permanent care decisions or awaiting community packages, but remained classified as Short Breaks rather than being reclassified. The service is undertaking reclassification work to separate planned, emergency and interim Short Breaks to improve accuracy of budgeting and management information, due by 31 May 2027.
findings.matters: Accurate classification of service expenditure is essential for reliable budget management and financial reporting; misclassification obscures true cost drivers and prevents proper service planning.
findings.figures: Extended periods ranging from five to sixteen months
findings.quote: Audit testing identified expenditure recorded as Short Break provision which, on further analysis, related to individuals remaining in residential accommodation for extended periods ranging from five to sixteen months.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Social Care (Short Breaks)
findings.headline: The council has no formal charging policy for Short Break provision and charged no eligible service users in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Scottish Government guidance (CRAG) permits local authorities to charge for Short Break respite services. The audit identified that no financial assessments were undertaken in 2025/26, leaving all charges unlevied. Audit testing found cases eligible for charging, including extended stays spanning several months, but these were not charged. Management has accepted the recommendation to develop a charging policy and formed a working group to progress this, due for implementation by 31 May 2027.
findings.matters: A council not recovering permissible revenue represents suboptimal financial management; other local authorities have implemented charging policies for similar services, demonstrating this is operationally feasible.
findings.figures: £517,000 annual budget for accommodated Short Breaks (older persons' care); zero charges levied in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Authority currently has no charging policy in place for Short Break provision. The audit identified that no referrals for financial assessment were undertaken in respect of Short Break provision during the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Management of School Funds
findings.headline: School Fund Regulations last updated April 2021 lack a formal review cycle and audit visits found staff were not aware of them.
findings.detail: The audit found the Regulations remain broadly fit for purpose but lack a defined review schedule and regular reissue process. Testing identified areas requiring updates, including Value Added Tax guidance. An audit visit to a school found a Head Teacher and School Administrator were not aware of the Regulations, though staffing changes were acknowledged as a factor.
findings.matters: Outdated regulations and poor staff awareness create conditions where non-compliance is likely to persist unless the council actively communicates and reinforces requirements.
findings.figures: Regulations last reviewed and updated April 2021; no formal review cycle in place
findings.quote: The Regulations were last reviewed and updated in April 2021... an audit visit to a school found that a Head Teacher and the School Administrator were not aware of the School Fund Regulations.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Management of School Funds
findings.headline: Five schools had not submitted required annual financial returns when the audit was conducted; one school also missed the prior year's submission.
findings.detail: The audit found that five schools had not submitted Annual Statements of Accounts and Bank Reconciliation Statements for 2024/25, with one school also failing to submit 2023/24 returns (both due by 1 November). Additionally, 22 schools (18 primary and 4 secondary) submitted late, with delays of one to three months. Four primary schools' statements lacked independent audit certification and 11 schools submitted incomplete returns.
findings.matters: Non-submission and late submission of required financial returns shows weak compliance monitoring by Education Services and suggests limited oversight of school financial management.
findings.figures: 5 schools did not submit 2024/25 returns; 1 also missed 2023/24; 22 schools submitted late (1–3 months); deadline 1 November 2025
findings.quote: At the time of the audit, five schools had not submitted their Annual Statement of Accounts and Bank Reconciliation Statements for 2024/25. In addition, one of these schools had also failed to submit the required financial returns for 2023/24.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Management of School Funds
findings.headline: A school paid £1,200 to a staff member as a salary advance from school funds, breaching both School Fund Regulations and Council Financial Regulations.
findings.detail: The audit found a £1,200 payment to a staff member described as a 'staff advancement' arising from a contractual change delay. This violated School Fund Regulations (which prohibit salary payments) and Council Financial Regulation 3.10 (which requires all payroll through the council's payroll system to ensure proper income tax and National Insurance accounting). The amount was reimbursed to the school fund approximately two months after the payment was made.
findings.matters: A breach of Council Financial Regulations on core payroll controls indicates control failures extend beyond school-specific procedures and affect how the council enforces its own regulations.
findings.figures: £1,200; reimbursed approximately two months after initial payment
findings.quote: This arrangement is not in accordance with the Council's Financial Regulations, specifically Regulation 3.10, which states: 'All individuals employed by the Council under a contract of service shall be paid through the payroll system to ensure proper accounting for Income Tax and National Insurance is made.'

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Home to School Transport
findings.headline: Contract extensions were not properly documented: no Letters of Variation in place for 2024-25 extensions, only approximately 40% signed for 2025-26 extensions.
findings.detail: Contract extensions should be formally documented through Letters of Variation agreed and signed by all parties. The audit found zero Letters of Variation in place for the 2024-25 extension and only partial documentation (approximately 40% of service providers with signed Letters of Variation) for the 2025-26 extension. A revised template has been created and management committed to full documentation going forward by 31 July 2026.
findings.matters: Incomplete contractual documentation creates risk of disputes and enforceability questions, and indicates weak contract management controls.
findings.figures: 0% of extensions formally documented in 2024-25; approximately 40% in 2025-26
findings.quote: Audit testing identified that no Letters of Variation were in place for contract extensions implemented during 2024–25, and that only partial documentation was obtained for extensions in 2025–26, with signed Letters of Variation available for approximately 40% of service providers.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Home to School Transport
findings.headline: No formal ongoing process exists to verify that home to school transport providers maintain required insurance cover throughout the duration of their contracts.
findings.detail: While insurance is verified at contract award, the audit found no ongoing annual assurance process that insurance remains valid and compliant throughout the contract period. This creates exposure to uninsured claims and leaves the council vulnerable to financial and reputational risk from incidents involving approximately 2,700 pupils. Management has accepted the recommendation to implement annual insurance verification by 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Uninsured claims from transport incidents would create direct financial exposure and safeguarding liability for the council.
findings.figures: Service covers approximately 2,700 pupils; no annual checks in place since 2019 contract start
findings.quote: While verification of transport providers' insurance documentation is undertaken at the point of contract award, the audit review identified that no ongoing process is in place to obtain annual assurance that insurance cover remains valid and compliant with contractual requirements throughout the contract period.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Home to School Transport
findings.headline: A contract variation for home to school transport worth £86,450 annually was awarded without following required procurement procedures or consulting the Chief Financial Officer.
findings.detail: Sample testing of four contract variations found one (annual value approximately £86,450) did not comply with the Council's Procurement Guidelines or Financial Regulations. The procedure that should have required formal tendering was bypassed. While alternative quotations were obtained and operational urgency acknowledged, the formal compliance requirements were not met and required CFO consultation was not undertaken.
findings.matters: This demonstrates a control breakdown in procurement governance, creating exposure to challenge, legal risk, and reputational damage.
findings.figures: £86,450 annual contract value
findings.quote: In the sample reviewed, one contract variation was found to not comply with the Procurement Guidelines. The annual value of this contract variation was approximately £86,450, which required the procurement of transport providers through a tendering exercise.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Home to School Transport
findings.headline: Council may owe approximately £10,000 to home to school transport providers due to contract uplift rate discrepancy in 2025/26.
findings.detail: A Letter of Variation specified a 3.2% annual uplift (calculated as 2.2% plus 1%), but the Chief Financial Officer advised applying March 2025 CPI at 3%. The lower rate was applied in actual payments, creating an estimated underpayment of £10,000 to transport providers. The audit recommends Legal Services determine whether the contractually-specified 3.2% rate applies and whether retrospective payment is required.
findings.matters: This represents a potential financial obligation that may require remediation and affects cash flow forecasting.
findings.figures: £10,000 underpayment; 3% applied versus 3.2% contractual specification
findings.quote: Analysis found that applying the lower rate has resulted in an estimated underpayment of approximately £10,000 to home to school transport providers.

findings.paper_title: Housing, Property and Communities Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: £54k Scottish Welfare Fund overspend requiring drawdown from earmarked reserves
findings.detail: The Scottish Welfare Fund (part of a wider £74k Benefits & Money Advice overspend) has exceeded budget by £54k due to higher activity levels. The council will cover this from earmarked reserves, showing service demand growth outpacing budgeted provision.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown signals welfare spending is unsustainable at budgeted levels; demonstrates service demand exceeding policy expectations.
findings.figures: £54k Scottish Welfare Fund overspend met from reserves
findings.quote: There is an overall overspend of £74k, predominantly arising from an overspend of £54k in the Scottish Welfare Fund due to higher activity levels, but which will subsequently be met from a balance of earmarked reserves.

findings.paper_title: Housing, Property and Communities Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Housing Benefits budget structurally underfunded, creating baseline overspends
findings.detail: Housing Benefits shows a £15k Q1 overspend. The council explicitly states this "arises from a historically low budget provision which is subject to review"—acknowledging the budget was never set at a sustainable level for actual demand.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off variance but a structural mismatch between service demand and budget; signals ongoing pressure that cannot be managed within current provision.
findings.figures: £15k Housing Benefits overspend from historically low budget
findings.quote: An overspend of £15k in Housing Benefits arises from a historically low budget provision which is subject to review

findings.paper_title: Housing, Property and Communities Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: £1,277k savings target includes £926k from capitalising PFI lifecycle costs, not operational savings
findings.detail: Only £75k of £1,277k proposed savings have been delivered by end Q1. The largest single item is £926k from capitalising PFI lifecycle costs—an accounting reclassification, not real expenditure reduction. Another £1,059k is expected in Q2, with £143k still under review to confirm whether already "baselined" into existing budgets.
findings.matters: Real operational savings and accounting treatments are not equivalent; relying on capitalisation to balance budgets signals potential structural underfunding; actual delivery rate is 6% to date.
findings.figures: £1,277k proposed savings, £75k posted, £926k capitalising PPP lifecycle costs, £1,059k expected Q2, £143k under review
findings.quote: Work on the proposed savings for Elgin Community Centre (£40k), Homelessness/allocations recharges from resettlement (£25k), Capitalising PPP lifecycle costs (£926k) and Smarter Working (£68k) remains ongoing, with the majority expected to be posted in the course of Quarter 2

findings.paper_title: Housing, Property and Communities Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: £191k HRA rental income loss from EPC discount delays in housing improvement programme
findings.detail: House rents are £191k below budget in Q1 because more tenancies are retaining an Energy Performance Certificate discount pending completion of energy efficiency works on their properties. The council notes progress is being reviewed in Q2, meaning the works are behind schedule.
findings.matters: HRA is self-financing through rents; delays in capital works create income volatility and signal the housing improvement programme may be running behind schedule.
findings.figures: £191k rental income shortfall
findings.quote: This predominantly arises from £191k less in rental income, attributable to a higher number of tenancies retaining the EPC discount, pending completion of energy improvement works.

findings.paper_title: Scottish Social Housing Charter Compliance
findings.headline: Electrical safety compliance gap of 11.4% requiring external contractor to address backlog of Category 2 faults
findings.detail: Only 5,718 of 6,457 properties (88.6%) hold compliant Electrical Installation Condition Reports as of 31 March 2026. Council has appointed an external contractor to assist with completion of identified Category 2 faults. All Category 1 (most critical) faults were addressed immediately.
findings.matters: Safety compliance gap creates regulatory and liability risk; appointment of external contractor indicates cost pressure to remediate backlog and suggests internal resources insufficient to maintain compliance.
findings.figures: 5,718 of 6,457 properties (88.6%) compliant; 739 properties non-compliant (11.4%)
findings.quote: By 31 March 2026, 5,718 (88.6%) properties had compliant Electrical Installation Condition Report (EICR). We have recently appointed an external contractor to assist us with completion of identified C2 faults.

findings.paper_title: Scottish Social Housing Charter Compliance
findings.headline: 12 households breached unsuitable accommodation standards due to insufficient housing supply during 2025/26
findings.detail: Council placed 12 households in breach of unsuitable accommodation standards (extended stays in Bed and Breakfast) during 2025/26 due to insufficient supply. Paper explicitly states this was caused by two periods where supply could not meet demand and cites lack of new council housing supply as exacerbating factor.
findings.matters: Service delivery failure on statutory obligation indicates housing supply-demand imbalance and that council cannot meet need from existing stock or new supply. This signals financial pressure (cost of temporary accommodation) and operational/reputational risk.
findings.figures: 12 households; 300 households total with statutory duty to secure permanent accommodation
findings.quote: During 2025/26 there were 12 households breaching the Unsuitable Accommodations Order. This was a direct result of two periods where supply was insufficient to meet demand and resulted in extended stays in Bed and Breakfast accommodation. This was further exacerbated by the lack of new supply of council housing.

findings.paper_title: Scottish Social Housing Charter Compliance
findings.headline: Acknowledged increase in damp and mould within council housing requiring ongoing remedial investment
findings.detail: Council's Housing and Community Safety Committee has formally acknowledged an increase in damp and mould within the housing stock. Mitigation includes external and internal wall insulation, enhanced ventilation, and environmental monitoring. Remedial works described as ongoing with future interventions prioritised for higher-risk properties.
findings.matters: Damp and mould indicate underlying building defect issues requiring sustained capital investment; this is an asset condition problem that could affect housing viability and service quality; also creates liability exposure for the council.
findings.figures: Number of affected properties not quantified; affects portion of 6,457-unit portfolio
findings.quote: Our Housing and Community Safety Committee has acknowledged the increase in dampness and mould within council housing and is actively implementing a range of mitigation measures. These include the installation of external and internal wall insulation, enhanced ventilation systems, and environmental monitoring devices.

findings.paper_title: Scottish Social Housing Charter Compliance
findings.headline: £20.1m capital maintenance programme required to close housing standards compliance gaps
findings.detail: Council invests £20.1m in 2025/26 on capital works including wall insulation, cavity insulation, heating upgrades, and kitchen/bathroom work to close gaps in Scottish Housing Quality Standard (SHQS) compliance (currently 63.3%) and Energy Efficiency Standard (currently 76.6%). Council has set 90% target but paper does not disclose funding source or HRA financial impact.
findings.matters: Significant sustained capital investment need indicates HRA financial pressure and questions whether capital programme is adequately funded from the housing revenue account or requires additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £20.1m planned capital maintenance spend in 2025/26; 63.3% SHQS compliance (4,085 of 6,457 properties); 76.6% EESSH compliance (4,944 of 6,457 properties); up from 43.7% SHQS compliance previous year
findings.quote: The 2025/26 the planned capital maintenance spend was £20.1m. The capital works have delivered internal wall insulation, cavity wall insulation, loft top ups, heating upgrades Kitchen and bathroom upgrades, along with Solar panel installations across the housing portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Housing Investment Plan update to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Council disposing of housing asset because capital investment requirement (£646k) exceeds financial return
findings.detail: Reidhaven House, comprising six bedsits in a listed building, has been recommended for disposal. Condition surveys found significant capital investment of approximately £646,000 would be needed to achieve compliance with housing standards. The Better Homes Board concluded the limited rental return does not justify this expenditure.
findings.matters: Asset disposal for viability reasons is uncommon in housing; signals potential other marginal properties in the portfolio and reflects capital constraints in achieving compliance across stock
findings.figures: £646,000 estimated capital investment required for six properties
findings.quote: Following assessment of the significant capital investment required to achieve SHQS and EESSH compliance, together with the limited financial return associated with retention, the board recommended that the properties be declared surplus to Housing Revenue Account requirements.

findings.paper_title: Housing Investment Plan update to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Electrical upgrades budget overdrawn in Q1 due to compliance-driven remedial works
findings.detail: The revenue budget line for electrical upgrades shows £229k spent against a £150k allocation, creating a £79k overspend by end of Q1. This reflects additional EICR-identified remedial works needed to maintain statutory compliance on aging installations.
findings.matters: Budget overruns on essential compliance work indicate inadequate initial budget setting and suggest further unbudgeted costs may emerge as inspections continue across the stock
findings.figures: Electrical Upgrades: £150k budget, £229k spent, -£79k variance (153% of budget)
findings.quote: The electrical upgrades budget is currently overspent as a result of the renewal and remedial works identified through the EICR programme.

findings.paper_title: Housing Investment Plan update to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Housing stock compliance lags peer group by 13 percentage points, creating ongoing regulatory risk
findings.detail: As at 30 June 2026, only 67.16% of Moray's housing stock meets Scottish Housing Quality Standards, compared with 80% across peer councils. While EESSH compliance is at 77.95%, the gap suggests capital investment will need to accelerate to avoid regulatory scrutiny.
findings.matters: Regulatory failure on housing standards can trigger intervention and forces capital spending regardless of affordability; peer gap indicates relative underinvestment or delivery challenges
findings.figures: 67.16% of Moray stock meets SHQS vs 80% of peer group; EESSH at 77.95%
findings.quote: As of 30 June 2026, 67.16% of our stock met the SHQS, compared with 80% of our peer group.

findings.paper_title: Operations and Environment and Growth, Planning and Climate Capital and Revenue Budget Monitoring to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Design Consultancy £85k overspend in Q1 linked to staff vacancies reducing capital cost recovery
findings.detail: Design Consultancy shows £85k overspend in Q1 (budget £204k, actual £289k). The council attributes this to work undertaken earlier than expected combined with 'capital recharge target not being met due to staff vacancies', indicating staffing constraints are preventing recovery of costs to capital projects.
findings.matters: Staffing vacancies affecting technical services indicate capacity constraints that can impair the council's ability to deliver capital programmes and recover costs from those programmes, creating budget pressure.
findings.figures: Q1 budget £204k, actual £289k, overspend £85k; annual budget £1,223k
findings.quote: The overspend on the Design Consultancy revenue budget is due to work being undertaken earlier than expected and the capital recharge target not being met due to staff vacancies.

findings.paper_title: Operations and Environment and Growth, Planning and Climate Capital and Revenue Budget Monitoring to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Roads machinery hire income saving of £50k not achieved; compensated by cutting patching roads maintenance budget
findings.detail: A £50k saving based on hiring out roads machinery to external parties has not materialised as expected income. The council states 'Expected income has not materialised' but 'continues to promote the use of this machine' while meantime taking the £50k saving from the patching roads budget, forcing a service delivery cut rather than finding alternative efficiencies.
findings.matters: Failed savings plans where expected new income does not materialise indicate either forecasting issues or market conditions that do not support original assumptions, forcing compensating cuts to service delivery.
findings.figures: £50k saving target; roads management annual budget £5,472k
findings.quote: Expected income has not materialised. However, work continues to promote the use of this machine to others within the local area. The 50k saving has therefore been taken from the patching roads budget.

findings.paper_title: Operations and Environment and Growth, Planning and Climate Capital and Revenue Budget Monitoring to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Craigellachie Bridge expansion joint work forecast to exceed total budget with potential reallocation of other bridge projects
findings.detail: The Design Consultancy capital section flags that Craigellachie Bridge expansion joint replacement will likely exceed its total budget. Additional repair works were identified when the joint was uncovered, requiring a costed solution. The council indicates it may need to defer funding for other bridge projects to accommodate this overrun.
findings.matters: Capital cost overruns force reallocation of limited resources and signal either poor project scoping, cost inflation on infrastructure maintenance, or delivery risks that affect the capital plan's credibility.
findings.figures: Craigellachie Bridge budget £75k; total bridges capital budget £22k currently underspent
findings.quote: It is likely that the work at Craigellachie Bridge will exceed the total budget and funding for other bridge projects may need to be deferred to accommodate this budget increase.

findings.paper_title: Operations and Environment and Growth, Planning and Climate Capital and Revenue Budget Monitoring to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Harbours income shortfall from whisky production downturn creating £42k revenue gap in Q1
findings.detail: The Harbours service shows a £43k variance in Q1 due to income shortfall. The council identifies the primary cause as a downturn in whisky production affecting malt cargo throughput. The annual harbours budget is only £69k, making this a material proportional impact (roughly 60% of annual income).
findings.matters: A significant drop in council revenue due to external economic factors affects financial capacity and debt servicing ability; this represents demand destruction in a key local industry affecting council revenues.
findings.figures: Q1 actual income £14k against budgeted £56k; annual budget £69k; variance £42,605k
findings.quote: the biggest influence is the downturn in whisky production with the consequent reduction in malt cargo

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 (April 2026 – June 2026) Performance Report – Adult Services
findings.headline: Care service quality improved significantly, moving from bottom third to top third of national partnerships.
findings.detail: National performance indicator 17 ('Proportion of care services graded good (4) or better in Care Inspectorate inspections') improved from 73.8% to 86.2%, lifting Moray from the bottom third nationally to the top third. Across all 19 national indicators, Moray performed above the Scottish average on 14 indicators in this period, up from 8 in the previous reporting period.
findings.matters: This is a positive movement in service quality and regulatory standing. Improvement in national benchmarking is a good signal to lenders about service stability and governance, partially offsetting capacity and staffing concerns.
findings.figures: 73.8% to 86.2% (care service quality); 14 of 19 national indicators above Scottish average (previously 8 of 19)
findings.quote: Indicator 17 "Proportion of care services graded "good (4) or better in Care Inspectorate inspections" has shown a significant improvement from 73.8% to 86.2% and now in the top third of partnerships as opposed to the bottom third in previous years.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 (April 2026 – June 2026) Performance Report – Adult Services
findings.headline: 45% of strategic delivery plan actions delayed, including dependencies on NHS Grampian partners.
findings.detail: Of 69 actions in the 2025-28 Strategic Delivery Plan, only 56% were either complete or on track at end of Q1 2026/27: 16 complete (23%), 22 on track (32%), and 31 delayed (45%). The paper cites delays due to various causes including dependencies on collaborative work with partners across Grampian. The plan itself is being refreshed to allow additional time for partnership discussions and governance processes.
findings.matters: Strategy execution risk and lack of control over delivery timescales, particularly where dependent on external partners, signals weak partnership governance and raises questions about ability to deliver planned improvements.
findings.figures: 16 complete (23%); 22 on track (32%); 31 delayed (45%); 69 total actions
findings.quote: The remaining 31 actions were underway but experiencing delays for a variety of reasons, including dependencies on collaborative work with partners across Grampian.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 (April 2026 – June 2026) Performance Report – Adult Services
findings.headline: A&E attendance at highest level in three years; Partnership has commissioned investigation.
findings.detail: A&E attendance rate per 1,000 population increased to 23.7 in Q1 2026/27, the highest level since Q1 2023. The Partnership determined this is not due to population changes and has commissioned Public Health Scotland to investigate referral sources (self-referral, GP, NHS 111), demographic patterns, reasons for attendance, and locality.
findings.matters: Rising A&E attendance suggests either acute service stress or a gap in primary/community care that people are compensating for. It indicates system pressure and may require investment in alternatives to emergency care.
findings.quote: The rate has increased since Qtr 4 and is at the highest level since Qtr 1 2023.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 (April 2026 – June 2026) Performance Report – Adult Services
findings.headline: Psychological therapy access collapsed to 26%, missing the 90% national target by 64 points.
findings.detail: Performance in access to psychological therapy within 18 weeks fell sharply in Q1 2026/27 to 26%, down from 41% in Q4 2025/26. The paper attributes this to increased demand combined with funding and workforce constraints. Secondary care meets the 18-week target but primary care performance is well below it. The Partnership is reviewing triage processes but acknowledges an 18-week lag before improvements will show.
findings.matters: This is a failure on a national priority indicator and signals insufficient mental health capacity. It suggests budget or staffing constraints are binding and will create pressure for additional investment.
findings.quote: Performance improved from March to 56% in April and 48% in May, before falling to 26% in June.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 (April 2026 – June 2026) Performance Report – Adult Services
findings.headline: Care at home waiting list growing with 30% of people waiting over six months for assessed care.
findings.detail: The number of people assessed and waiting for a care package increased during Q1 2026/27, alongside unmet hours of care. At the end of Q1, 29.7% of the 195 people on the waiting list (58 individuals) had been waiting for more than six months for an assessed care package. The paper attributes unmet need to increasing demand, workforce and provider capacity challenges, and growing complexity of care needs.
findings.matters: Long waits for assessed care create safeguarding risks and potential legal exposure. It indicates the council cannot meet eligible need and is rationing access by making people wait, creating reputational and financial risk.
findings.figures: 58 of 195 people waiting 6+ months (29.7%)
findings.quote: For some people, the length of time waiting for care can be significant. At the end of Qtr 1 29.7% of people (58 of 195) had been waiting for more than six months.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 (April 2026 – June 2026) Performance Report – Adult Services
findings.headline: Delayed discharges hit red threshold at 37, driven by shortage of care home places.
findings.detail: Delayed discharges increased to 37 in Q1 2026/27, exceeding the target of 26 and entering red status (more than 5% above target). The paper identifies lack of available care and care home placement as a significant blocking issue. Bed days occupied by delayed discharges reached 1,311 in Q1 2026/27, above the target of 850. Additional support and resources have been directed to address blockages.
findings.matters: This is an acute operational crisis affecting hospital capacity and system flow, indicating the council cannot commission or provide sufficient downstream care capacity. It signals both a service delivery failure and potential budget pressure from emergency measures.
findings.figures: 37 delayed discharges (target 26); 1,311 bed days occupied (target 850); Q4 2025/26: 34 delayed discharges
findings.quote: Delayed Discharges increased during the period levelling at 37 which is into the red threshold resulting in additional support and resource being directed to try to address any blockages. A significant issue is the lack of available care and care home placement available.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 (April 2026 – June 2026) Performance Report – Adult Services
findings.headline: Council staff sickness absence surged to 10% in one quarter, driven by mental health crises.
findings.detail: Council staff sickness absence jumped from 8.5% in Q4 2025/26 to 10% in Q1 2026/27. Days lost increased by 769 from the same quarter last year, with long-term absence accounting for 666 of those days. Absence specifically attributed to depression, stress and anxiety rose 66% quarter-on-quarter. Senior Management flagged this as an area of concern and is investigating root causes.
findings.matters: A sharp deterioration in staff wellbeing is a red flag for organisational dysfunction or burnout. It will degrade service delivery and create financial pressure through overtime, locum cover, and reduced productivity.
findings.figures: 10% Q1 2026/27 (vs 8.5% Q4 2025/26); 3703 days lost (vs 2934 Q1 2025/26); 375-day increase in depression/stress/anxiety-related absence (66% increase)
findings.quote: Council employed staff absences showed from Q1 2025/26 to Q1 2026/27 that days lost from sickness increased from 2934 to 3703 (769 days), most of these (666 days) were increases in "long term days". Of the 3703 days absence, 69% (2554) related to long term days lost in Q1 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Report to Those Charged with Governance
findings.headline: Auditors have identified financial sustainability as a significant risk in their audit risk assessment, questioning the IJB's ability to deliver required transformation.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton explicitly identifies financial sustainability as a significant risk. The auditors conclude: 'To achieve long-term financial sustainability, the IJB must successfully deliver its savings and transformation programme...Failure to achieve planned savings and transformation outcomes could result in significant financial pressures and increase the risk to the IJB's financial sustainability.'
findings.matters: The auditors' own risk assessment confirms that the IJB's long-term financial viability depends on delivering a transformation programme that has not yet been proven or detailed. This is the auditor's way of flagging structural insolvency risk.
findings.figures: Significant risk identified in audit planning; Medium Term Financial Framework projects £39m cumulative gap
findings.quote: There remains a significant risk in respect of financial sustainability given the significant financial challenges the IJB faces over the longer term

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Report to Those Charged with Governance
findings.headline: Older People Services overspent by £1.933 million due to shift toward higher-acuity nursing care, reflecting worsening demographic pressures.
findings.detail: The IJB faces an increasing older population coupled with a declining working-age population. Clients are shifting from residential to nursing care, raising unit costs. The auditors note 'an increasing older population, coupled with a declining working-age population...is placing growing demand on services.'
findings.matters: This is a structural cost driver that will not reverse. As the population ages, the proportion of high-acuity, high-cost clients will grow, making the funding gap worse.
findings.figures: Older People Services and Physical & Sensory Disability overspend: £1.933m
findings.quote: The overspend of £1.933 million primarily related to overspends for home care and permanent care due to the increase in clients receiving nursing care rather than residential care

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Report to Those Charged with Governance
findings.headline: Q1 2026/27 position shows £1.6 million overspend by end of June and forecast full-year deficit of £8.975 million, with auditors stating savings delivery is 'unlikely'.
findings.detail: Despite the £9 million planned deficit funding, the IJB is already off track. Auditors report: 'It is unlikely that the IJB will deliver all required savings in 2026/27 and will review alternative options to help reduce the projected deficit.' Only £4.1m of £5.7m required savings are rated as likely to be achieved.
findings.matters: 2026/27 is already projecting to exceed the planned deficit envelope before Q1 is complete. This shows the underlying structural deficit is worsening faster than anticipated.
findings.figures: Core Services overspend to date (June 2026): £1.615m; Strategic Funds: £0.358m; forecast full-year deficit: £8.975m (3.8% of budget); savings at risk: £1.6m of £5.7m target
findings.quote: The budget position at the end of June 2026 is an overspend to date on the Core Services budget of £1.615 million, and an overspend on the Strategic Funds budget of £0.358 million

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Report to Those Charged with Governance
findings.headline: Internal Audit has issued a limited assurance opinion for five consecutive years, indicating unresolved governance and control weaknesses.
findings.detail: The auditors note this is 'unusual' and reflects 'ongoing weaknesses in the framework of governance, risk management and control.' Multiple internal audit recommendations remain outstanding across multiple years. The pace of resolution has been insufficient.
findings.matters: Five consecutive years of limited assurance signals weak internal controls, increased fraud risk, and reliability issues with financial reporting. This is a governance red flag.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years limited assurance (2021/22–2025/26); 8 prior recommendations tracked, 5 closed, 3 remaining open
findings.quote: This is the fifth year in succession that Internal Audit have provided a limited assurance opinion

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Report to Those Charged with Governance
findings.headline: IJB holds zero general reserves; all £3 million in reserves are earmarked for specific purposes.
findings.detail: The IJB has no contingency reserves. The auditors explicitly state: 'While the 2026/27 budget does not rely on the use of general reserves, the absence of an uncommitted reserve balance limits the IJB's ability to respond to emerging risks and funding uncertainties.' Any future overspend must be funded by partners.
findings.matters: Zero reserves means the IJB is vulnerable to any shock—a service demand spike, cost inflation, staffing emergency. All such pressures flow directly to partners.
findings.figures: Total reserves 31 March 2026: £3.010m (all earmarked); general reserves balance: £0m
findings.quote: The IJB general reserves balance is nil, meaning future overspends would need to be fully met by the partner authorities, as all available reserves are earmarked

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Report to Those Charged with Governance
findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap projected at £39 million from 2026/27 to 2030/31, representing a significant increase from previous projections.
